power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Samples with balanced quotas for age (five categories: 20% 18-29 years, 20% 30-39 years, 20% 40-49 years, 20% 50-59 years, 20% 60 years and older) and gender (two categories: 50% male, 50% female) were collected by the market research company Bilendi & respondi with the use of online questionnaires programmed in Qualtrics ten days before and three weeks after the referendum on June 18, 2023. Sample size was determined based on a power analysis for a different, non-overlapping paper (see pre-registration and Cologna et al., 2024). We also considered expected attrition and failure rates for the attention checks (two in the pre-referendum and one in the post-referendum survey). A power analysis for using a paired-samples t-test indicated that a total sample size of approximately 198 participants would be required to detect a small effect size (Cohen's d = 0.2) with 80% power at a 5% significance level (two-tailed). Our sample of 827 participants clearly exceeds this number.

table.title: How collective policy advocacy affects trust in scientists: A case study of the Swiss Climate Protection Law
table.research_questions:
RQ1a: What is the level of support (voting intentions) for the CPL at T2?

RQ1b: Which variables influence support (voting intentions) for the CPL at T2?
H1b: Support for the CPL at T2 is associated with the following variables: (1) trust in scientists at T1, (2) party preference (SVP vs other), (3) political orientation, (4) climate change concern, (5) condition (treatment vs. control), (6) gender, (7) being a father to a daughter, (8) language region, (9) urban/rural, (10) age, (11) income

RQ2a: Is there a statistically significant difference in trust in scientists between the control group and treatment group at T2?
H2a: Trust in scientists will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T2.

RQ2b: Do political orientation and party preference (SVP vs. others) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on trust in scientists at T2?
H2b: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on trust in scientists among SVP supporters and more right-leaning individuals at T2. 

RQ2c: Is there a statistically significant difference in the normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking between the control group and treatment group at T2?
H2c: Normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T2.

RQ2d: Do political orientation and party preference (SVP vs. others) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking at T2?
H2d: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking among SVP supporters and more right-leaning individuals at T2. 

RQ2e: Is there a statistically significant difference in the voting intentions between the control group and treatment group at T2?
H2e: Voting intentions will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T2.

RQ2f: Do political orientation and party preference (SVP vs. others) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on voting intentions at T2?
H2f: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on voting intentions among SVP supporters and more right-leaning individuals at T2. 


RQ3a: Is there a statistically significant difference in trust in scientists between the control group and treatment group at T3?
H3a: Trust in scientists will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T3.

RQ3b: Does voting behavior (yes vs. no) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on trust in scientists at T3?
H3b: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on trust in scientists for participants who voted against the CPL at T3. 

RQ3c: Is there a statistically significant difference in normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking between the control group and treatment group at T3?
H3c: Normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking will be significantly higher in the treatment group than in the control group at T3. 

RQ3d: Does voting behavior (yes vs. no) moderate the effect of treatment vs. control on normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking at T3?
H3d: We hypothesize a negative effect of treatment vs. control on normative perceptions of scientists in policymaking for participants who voted against the CPL at T3. 


RQ4: Does observing the voting outcome influence a) normative perceptions, b) trust in science, c) support for climate change policies and d) beliefs about the views of other people in Switzerland at T3? (Treatment: showing each participant the voting result for their canton/voting district)
H4: Observing a YES vote increases a) normative perceptions, b) trust in science, c) support for climate change policies and d) beliefs about other people’s support for the CPL and for scientists advocacy, and about their concern about climate change


RQ5a: What is participants’ perceived level of support for the CPL among other people in Switzerland at T2?
H5a: The perceived level of support for the CPL among other people in Switzerland will be underestimated. 

RQ5b: What is participants’ perceived level of concern about climate change among other people in Switzerland at T2?
H5b: The perceived level of concern about climate change among other people in Switzerland will be underestimated. 

RQ5c: What is participants’ perceived level of support for scientists’ climate policy advocacy among other people in Switzerland at T2?
H5c: The perceived level of support for scientists’ climate policy advocacy among other people in Switzerland will be underestimated.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview: Our study is a longitudinal online survey in Switzerland with an experiment embedded in the survey. In February 2023, data from n = 1,018 Swiss participants was collected (Time 1). In June 2023, participants who completed the survey in Time 1 will be invited to complete a survey with an embedded experiment in which participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions: control vs. treatment (Time 2). We will additionally recruit more participants who will also randomly be assigned to one of the two conditions to ensure adequate sample size/statistical power given the anticipated attrition between waves. All participants who completed the survey at Time 2 will also be invited to participate in a third online study with an embedded experiment in June 2023 (Time 3), in which participants will be assigned to the same condition (control vs. treatment) as in Time 2.
table.randomization: Participants will randomly be assigned to either a control or a treatment condition at Time 2 and reassigned to the same condition at Time 3.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.existing_data_explanation: For some analyses, we will use data collected at Time 1 (before any manipulation occurred).
table.data_collection_procedures:
We will collect data in two online surveys with experiments embedded in Switzerland in June 2023. The first survey will be conducted before 18 June 2023 and the second after 18 June 2023. 

Respondents will be recruited from an online panel provided by the market research company Bilendi & Respondi. Respondents will receive vouchers/credit points for completing the full survey, which they can redeem and/or transfer into money. 

In order to be able to complete the survey, respondents must:
- Agree with the terms and conditions of the consent form
- Be at least 18 years old
- Pass a first attention check, which asks them to write “213” in a text box
- Pass a second attention check, which asks them to indicate a) How many signatures are needed to launch a popular initiative in the control group; b) How many scientists signed a statement in support of the climate protection law in the treatment group. 
- At T3, pass one attention check, which asks them to write “600” in a text box.
table.sample_size:
In Study 1 (Time 2 - pre-voting), we will invite n = 1,018 participants who participated in our survey in February 2023 (Time 1) to complete our online survey. According to the market research company Bilendi & Respondi, we can expect a recall rate of about 60%, i.e., about n = 600. We will additionally recruit n = 1,050 for a total sample of n = 1,650 at Time 2.

In Study 2 (Time 3 - post-voting), we will invite all participants that completed Study 1 (Time 2- pre-voting). With a recall rate of about 60% (and excluding participants that failed our attention checks at Time 2), we expect to be able to recruit n = 891 at Time 3.
table.sample_size_rationale:
We used the software program G*Power to conduct a power analysis. Our goal was to obtain .80 power to detect a small effect size d = 0.20 at the standard .05 alpha error probability. Our power analysis shows that a sample of n = 788 is needed to have 80% power to detect a small effect size d = 0.20 for our independent t-tests (two-tailed). Given that we want participants at Time 3 to have completed the questionnaire at Time 2, and we can expect a recall rate of about 60%, a sample of at least n = 1,313 at Time 2 is needed in order to have about n = 788 participants at Time 3. As we have two attention checks in our survey at Time 2 (with an expected 10% failure rate in total), and another attention check at Time 3 (with an expected 10% failure rate), we aim to recruit n = 1,650 at Time 2. We expect to be able to resample about n = 600 participants from Time 1 at Time 2 and will invite an additional n = 1,050 to complete our survey at Time 2. All participants at Time 2 (pre-voting), will then be recontacted to fill out our survey at Time 3 (post-voting). 

Recruitment overview:

Time 2: Resampled from Time 1 (at a 60% resampling rate) → n = 600
Time 2: Recruitment of additional sample of n = 1,050
Time 2: Final sample post attention check fails (assuming 10% failure rate) → n = 1,485

Time 3: Resampled from Time 2 (at a 60% resampling rate) → n = 891
Time 3: Final sample post attention check fails (assuming 10% failure rate) → n = 802
table.stopping_rule: In T2, data collection will be stopped as soon as the target sample size of n = 1,485 has been reached. In T3, data collection will be stopped as soon as the target sample size of n = 788 has been reached.
table.manipulated_variables: We manipulate the information that participants receive in the treatment versus control condition. In T2, participants in the control condition receive an explanatory text on popular initiatives, are informed that the climate protection law is an example of a counter-proposal to a popular initiative and that it enjoys large support among politicians, businesses, and associations. Participants in the treatment condition at T2 receive a text that includes original statements taken from a letter signed by over 230 scientists in support of the climate protection law. Participants in the treatment condition at T3 receive three sentences that state that scientists were either advocating for a law supported by the majority of the public or not, depending on the outcome of the voting. The control condition will not see any additional information.
table.measured_variables:
We will measure the following variables (see also questionnaires attached):

Climate change concern: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

Pluralistic ignorance: 3 items, Item 1 measured with a slider from 0-100%, Item 2 measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much), Item 3 measured with a five-point scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)

Trust government: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

Social trust: Binary measure (0 = People can be trusted, 1 = You can't be too careful when dealing with others)

Awareness of CPL: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very familiar)

Representativeness of scientists: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very strongly)

Objectivity of scientists: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = strongly strongly)

Voting intentions: Categorical measure (0 = Yes, 1 = No, 2 = I would abstain, 3 = I am not sure)

Acceptability of law: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = measures are too strong, 5 = measures are too weak, 99 = Don’t know)

Support for future climate protection laws: 1 item, measured with a five-point scale (1 = not at all, 5 = very much)

Trust in scientists: 12 items on 4 dimensions, measured with five-point scales (1 = very inexpert, very unintelligent, very unqualified, etc. to 5 = very expert, very intelligent, very qualified, etc.):
Competence
- How expert or inexpert are most scientists?
- How intelligent or unintelligent are most scientists?
- How qualified or unqualified are most scientists when it comes to conducting high-quality - research?
Integrity
- How honest or dishonest are most scientists?
- How ethical or unethical are most scientists?
- How sincere or insincere are most scientists?
Benevolence
- How concerned or not concerned are most scientists about people’s wellbeing?
- How eager or uneager are most scientists to improve others’ lives?
- How considerate or inconsiderate are most scientists of others’ interests?
Openness
- How open are most scientists to feedback?
- How willing or unwilling are most scientists to be transparent?
- How much or little attention do scientists pay to others' views?

Normative perceptions of the role of science in society and politics: 5 items asking for the level agreement with five statements, measured with 5-point scales (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree)
- Scientists should work closely with politicians to integrate scientific results into policy-making.
- Scientists should actively advocate for specific policies.
- Scientists should communicate their findings to politicians.
- Scientists should be more involved in the policy-making process.
- Scientists should communicate about science with the general public.

Participated in voting: Binary measure (0 = Yes, 1 = No)

Actual voting behavior: Categorical measure (0 = Yes, 1 = No, 2 = Prefer not to say)

Reasons for not voting: Categorical measure (0 = I wanted to abstain, 1 = I was unsure what to vote, 2 = I am not eligible to vote in Switzerland, 3 = Other (please describe))

Gender: Categorical measure (0 = female, 1 = male, 2 = prefer to self-describe, 99 = prefer not to say)

Age: Metric measure (in years)

Educational attainment: Categorical measure (0 = did not attend school, 1 = primary education, 2 = secondary education, 3 = higher education)

Region of origin: Categorical measure (0 = Switzerland, 1 = European Union/EFTA, 2 = Other (third states)

Canton of residence: List with all cantons

Language region: Categorical measure (0 = German, 1 = Italian, 2 = French, 3 = Romansh) 

Voting eligibility: Categorical measure (0 = Yes, 1 = No, 2 = Don’t know)

Income: Metric measure (household’s yearly net income in local currency)

Urban/rural region of residence: Binary measure (1 = rural, 2 = urban)

Political orientation: 1 item asking respondents to self-classify as left-leaning or right-leaning, measured with a 5-point scale (1 = strongly left-leaning to 5 = strongly right-leaning)

Party preference: Categorical measure (0 = SVP, 1 = SP, 2 = FDP, 3 = GPS, 4 = GLP, 5 = The Centre, 6 = EVP, 7 = FDU, 8 = Ensemble à gauche, 9 = Lega dei Ticinesi, 10 = Other (please describe), 99 = I don’t know)

Religiosity: 1 item asking respondents to report the extent to which they consider themselves as religious, measured with a 5-point scale (1 = not religious at all to 5 = very strongly religious)

Parenthood: Binary measure (1 = Yes, 0 = No)

Gender of children: Categorical measure (0 = Boy, 1 = Girl, 2 = Both, I have more than one child, 99 = Prefer not to say)
table.indices:
We will use the following indices:
- Trust in scientists: Mean index of all 12 items measuring trust in scientists (see above)
- Normative perceptions of the role of science in society and politics: Mean index of all 5 items asking for normative perceptions (see above)

table.formatted: As hypothesized, pre-referendum participants significantly underestimated others' concern about climate change (actual: N = 1,578, M = 3.78, SD = 1.08, perceived: N = 1,578, M = 3.39, SD = 0.76, difference: 95% CI of mean difference [0.33-0.44], t(1577) = 13.41, d = .34, p < .001).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Careless Responding

926 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **665 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 7 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  2 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  15 installable dependencies detected.
- 1489 statistics stored from the extracted output; 5 of 22 reported tests matched (22.7%).

summary_table.ethics_statements: Therefore, the Harvard University Area Committee on the Use of Human Subjects determined that no further ethics approval was needed for this study.
live_data_statements: For a separate study (Cologna et al., 2024), participants were randomly assigned to a control or treatment condition in the pre-referendum study, but due to an error from the market research company, some participants were not reassigned to the same experimental condition post-referendum.

Finally, panel attrition checks, which examined whether baseline demographic, attitudinal and experimental variables predicted whether participants completed the post-referendum survey, showed that older participants and participants in the control (vs. treatment) condition used in the other study were more likely to remain in the study (see Table S2).

After answering questions on their own and others' climate change concern and others' support for scientists' advocacy in the pre-referendum survey, participants were randomly assigned to a control or a treatment condition (note that assignment to a treatment or control condition was for a different study).
In the post-referendum survey, participants were informed about the voting outcome in their canton of residence.
Participants were then asked about their own and others' concern about climate change and advocacy support.

We recruited a large sample that is representative of the Swiss population in terms of age, gender, and tertiary education, but may not be exactly representative for income and political orientation (see Table S1).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R", 
"CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric")), row.names = c(NA, -2L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**8 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_RESAMPLE.csv` to `../Datasets/ORIGINAL datasets_do-not-use/data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_RESAMPLE.csv` (in ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R); `data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_NEW.csv` to `../Datasets/ORIGINAL datasets_do-not-use/data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_NEW.csv` (in ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R); `data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_CONTROL.csv` to `../Datasets/ORIGINAL datasets_do-not-use/data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_CONTROL.csv` (in ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R); `data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_TREATMENT.csv` to `../Datasets/ORIGINAL datasets_do-not-use/data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_TREATMENT.csv` (in ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R); `data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_RESAMPLE_corrected.xlsx` to `../Datasets/CORRECTED datasets/data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_RESAMPLE_corrected.xlsx` (in CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R); `data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_NEW_corrected.xlsx` to `../Datasets/CORRECTED datasets/data_CPLadvocacy-pre-vote_NEW_corrected.xlsx` (in CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R); `data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_CONTROL_corrected.xlsx` to `../Datasets/CORRECTED datasets/data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_CONTROL_corrected.xlsx` (in CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R); `data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_TREATMENT_corrected.xlsx` to `../Datasets/CORRECTED datasets/data_CPLadvocacy-post-vote_TREATMENT_corrected.xlsx` (in CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R", 
"CORRECTED_CPL_advocacy_24JUN25_newIDs.R"), Outcome = c("ran_ok", 
"ran_ok"), Detail = c("", ""), "Time (s)" = c(11.6, 12.7)), row.names = c(NA, 
-2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "ORIGINAL_do-not-use_CPL_advocacy_06DEC24.R", 
    "setwd() removed" = 1L, "Path(s) it set" = "(non-literal)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: Pluralistic ignorance about others' climate change concern can contribute to inaction on climate change.
We conducted a two-wave panel study (Npre = 1,578, Npost = 827) with a general sample before and after the national Swiss referendum on the Climate Protection Law, which was accepted.
We find that people underestimate others' concern about climate change and others' support of scientists' policy advocacy.
Pluralistic ignorance of climate change concern slightly decreased after the referendum, while pluralistic ignorance of scientists' advocacy remained unchanged.
Results thus show that national voting on climate policy creates a window of opportunity that can be harnessed to reduce pluralistic ignorance.

referendum on the Swiss Climate Protection Law and found that study participants held more accurate perceptions of other people's concern about climate change after learning that most voters supported the law in the referendum.
Perceptions about others' support for scientists' public advocacy remained unchanged.
This shows that pluralistic ignorance was reduced and people's beliefs about what others think became more accurate.
Holding a referendum about a policy can therefore change people's perceptions of others, perhaps because they see the vote as a signal about others' values.

Thus, researchers and policy makers should not overlook the potential power of public policy referenda for improving peoples' misperceptions about others' beliefs about critical challenges like climate change.
Pluralistic ignorance occurs when people underestimate others' broader agreement with their stance (S. J. Geiger et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Pluralistic ignorance occurs when people underestimate others' broader agreement with their stance (S. J. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Geiger et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Such ignorance can be a major challenge for collective action and public support for climate protection policies (N. Geiger & Swim, 2016).
text.formatted: Such ignorance can be a major challenge for collective action and public support for climate protection policies (N. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Geiger & Swim, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Pluralistic ignorance has been shown in contexts such as societal gender norms (Bicchieri, 2017; Bursztyn et al., 2023), drinking norms on college campuses (Prentice & Miller, 1993), political polarization (Ahler, 2014), same-sex marriage and parenting (Eisner et al., 2021), and tax evasion (Bergolo et al., 2020; Bursztyn & Yang, 2022).
text.formatted: Pluralistic ignorance has been shown in contexts such as societal gender norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bicchieri, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bursztyn et al., 2023)</ref>, drinking norms on college campuses <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Prentice & Miller, 1993)</ref>, political polarization <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahler, 2014)</ref>, same-sex marriage and parenting <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Eisner et al., 2021)</ref>, and tax evasion <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bergolo et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bursztyn & Yang, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Other studies have begun to document pluralistic ignorance in the context of climate change beliefs and policies, such as a survey on undergraduate students in the United States (U.S.) (N. Geiger & Swim, 2016), a recent survey in 20 countries (Dechezleprêtre et al., 2022), and a global survey study (Andre et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Other studies have begun to document pluralistic ignorance in the context of climate change beliefs and policies, such as a survey on undergraduate students in the United States (U.S.) (N. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Geiger & Swim, 2016)</ref>, a recent survey in 20 countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dechezleprêtre et al., 2022)</ref>, and a global survey study <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andre et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In general, these studies suggest strong evidence of pluralistic ignorance about others' concern for climate change and others' support for climate change mitigation policies in several countries (Andre et al., 2024), including the U.S. (Sparkman et al., 2022) and Switzerland (Andre et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In general, these studies suggest strong evidence of pluralistic ignorance about others' concern for climate change and others' support for climate change mitigation policies in several countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andre et al., 2024)</ref>, including the U.S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Sparkman et al., 2022)</ref> and Switzerland <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andre et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this widespread, strong evidence (see Miller, 2023; Sargent & Newman, 2021, for reviews), little is known about what can be done to reduce pluralistic ignorance, especially in the climate policy context (Constantino et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Despite this widespread, strong evidence (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Miller, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Sargent & Newman, 2021</ref>, for reviews), little is known about what can be done to reduce pluralistic ignorance, especially in the climate policy context <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Constantino et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Answering calls from scholars who have highlighted the value of testing interventions that can correct pluralistic ignorance (Sparkman et al., 2022), and building on evidence that elections can change personal attitudes and beliefs in other domains (Apffelstaedt et al., 2022; Bursztyn et al., 2020; Jung & Tavits, 2021), we use a naturally occurring event to explore the factors that reduce climate-related pluralistic ignorance.
text.formatted: Answering calls from scholars who have highlighted the value of testing interventions that can correct pluralistic ignorance <ref type="bibr">(Sparkman et al., 2022)</ref>, and building on evidence that elections can change personal attitudes and beliefs in other domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Apffelstaedt et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bursztyn et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Jung & Tavits, 2021)</ref>, we use a naturally occurring event to explore the factors that reduce climate-related pluralistic ignorance.

text.text: Specifically, we leverage the context of a national referendum on a climate protection law in 2023 in Switzerland.
In doing so, we replicate and extend these lines of research by providing field evidence for referendum effects in reducing pluralistic ignorance.
First, we replicated the finding of pluralistic ignorance in others' concern about climate change in a large Swiss general population sample.
Similarly, we found that pluralistic ignorance also existed around others' support for scientists' policy advocacy.
Together, these factors likely undermine a possible policy path to increase concern and knowledge around climate change in the population.
But finally-and criticallywe showed that an accepted referendum on climate protection significantly reduced pluralistic ignorance in others' concern about climate change.
We take advantage of the unique field setting of a referendum on a climate protection law in Switzerland.
On June 18, 2023, the Swiss electorate voted on the Federal Act on Climate Protection Targets, Innovation and Strengthening Energy Security (the "Climate Protection Law" or CPL).

The bill proposed an emission target and a path to reduce emissions gradually until 2050 together with subsidies and incentives to reduce energy consumption and invest in new climate-friendly technologies.
The CPL was accepted by a majority of the Swiss electorate (i.e., 59.1%).
Before the national vote, more than 230 scientists in Switzerland also organized to advocate in favor of the CPL, issuing a public statement supporting it.
The statement was signed by scientists across disciplines, from climate science to economics, social sciences and law.
Thus, our context involves not only a referendum, but also collective scientific advocacy in support of it.

To examine if pluralistic ignorance regarding climate change concern and support for scientists' policy advocacy is present in Switzerland, we pre-registered the following research questions and hypotheses: RQ1: What is participants' perceived level of concern about climate change among other people in Switzerland pre-vote?
H1: The perceived level of concern about climate change among other people in Switzerland will be underestimated.
RQ2: What is participants' perceived level of support for scientists' climate policy advocacy among other people in Switzerland pre-vote?
H2: The perceived level of support for scientists' climate policy advocacy among other people in Switzerland will be underestimated.

Moreover, to examine if perceptions were more accurate after the referendum (i.e., whether pluralistic ignorance was decreased), we pre-registered exploratory analyses to assess whether participants' perceptions of others' concern about climate change and support for scientists' policy advocacy pre-vote would be closer to actual levels of concern and policy support postvote.
We conducted a pre-registered, two-wave study with residents in Switzerland.

We pre-registered our research questions on OSF prior to data collection. 1 We collected data twice from the same sample of participants: in the ten days leading up to the referendum (N = 1,578) and about three weeks after the referendum (N = 827).
text.formatted: We pre-registered our research questions on OSF prior to data collection. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> We collected data twice from the same sample of participants: in the ten days leading up to the referendum (N = 1,578) and about three weeks after the referendum (N = 827).

text.text: Samples with balanced quotas for age (five categories: 20% 18-29 years, 20% 30-39 years, 20% 40-49 years, 20% 50-59 years, 20% 60 years and older) and gender (two categories: 50% male, 50% female) were collected by the market research company Bilendi & respondi with the use of online questionnaires programmed in Qualtrics ten days before and three weeks after the referendum on June 18, 2023.
text.formatted: Samples with balanced quotas for age (five categories: 20% 18-29 years, 20% 30-39 years, 20% 40-49 years, 20% 50-59 years, 20% 60 years and older) and gender (two categories: 50% male, 50% female) were collected by the market research company Bilendi & respondi with the use of online questionnaires programmed in Qualtrics ten days before and three weeks after the referendum on June 18, 2023.

text.text: Sample size was determined based on a power analysis for a different, non-overlapping paper (see pre-registration and Cologna et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Sample size was determined based on a power analysis for a different, non-overlapping paper (see pre-registration and <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cologna et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We also considered expected attrition and failure rates for the attention checks (two in the pre-referendum and one in the post-referendum survey).

A power analysis for using a paired-samples t-test indicated that a total sample size of approximately 198 participants would be required to detect a small effect size (Cohen's d = 0.2) with 80% power at a 5% significance level (two-tailed).
Our sample of 827 participants clearly exceeds this number.
Pre-referendum, we surveyed 1,892 participants.
2.74% of respondents failed the first attention check and 12.68% failed the second attention check, meaning they did not read the questions carefully.

We only retained responses of participants that passed both attention checks and completed the survey, resulting in a final sample of 1,578 participants pre-referendum after deleting 45 duplicate responses.
49.9% of our final pre-referendum sample identified as female and the mean age of our sample was 44 years. 43% indicated to have completed tertiary education.
Post-referendum, we reinvited all participants that had completed the pre-referendum survey, resulting in 961 participants.
We only retained responses of participants that passed the attention check and completed the survey, and deleted duplicate responses by keeping the first response.

For a separate study (Cologna et al., 2024), participants were randomly assigned to a control or treatment condition in the pre-referendum study, but due to an error from the market research company, some participants were not reassigned to the same experimental condition post-referendum.
text.formatted: For a separate study <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cologna et al., 2024)</ref>, participants were randomly assigned to a control or treatment condition in the pre-referendum study, but due to an error from the market research company, some participants were not reassigned to the same experimental condition post-referendum.

text.text: We deleted these responses, resulting in a final sample size of 827 participants.
45.94 % of our sample identified as female and the mean age of our sample was 48 years. 43 % indicated to have completed tertiary education.

Our samples are mostly representative of the Swiss population in terms of age, gender, and tertiary education, but may not be representative for income and political orientation (i.e., our sample appears to be below the Swiss net average household income and slightly more right-leaning than the Swiss average; Table S1).
text.formatted: Our samples are mostly representative of the Swiss population in terms of age, gender, and tertiary education, but may not be representative for income and political orientation (i.e., our sample appears to be below the Swiss net average household income and slightly more right-leaning than the Swiss average; Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: Finally, panel attrition checks, which examined whether baseline demographic, attitudinal and experimental variables predicted whether participants completed the post-referendum survey, showed that older participants and participants in the control (vs. treatment) condition used in the other study were more likely to remain in the study (see Table S2).

text.text: Although this affects the representativeness of the sample and thus, could undermine external validity, non-random attrition cannot affect the results of the t-tests, since we compare the responses of those who participated in both survey rounds (N = 827).
Results remain robust when controlling for age and treatment (see first column Tables S5-S8).
text.formatted: Results remain robust when controlling for age and treatment (see first column Tables <ref type="table">S5-S8</ref>).

text.text: Furthermore, neither experimental treatment (see second column Tables S5-S6) nor age (see second column Tables S7-S8) interacted with our main analyses to influence results.
text.formatted: Furthermore, neither experimental treatment (see second column Tables <ref type="table">S5-S6</ref>) nor age (see second column Tables <ref type="table">S7-S8</ref>) interacted with our main analyses to influence results.

text.text: To ensure that the random assignment to a control or treatment group did not affect our postreferendum results, we ran two exploratory, non-preregistered multilevel regression models with random intercepts across participants-one for advocacy support as outcome variable and one for climate change concern as outcome variable-with perceived vs. actual support of advocacy/concern, pre-vs. post-referendum, and treatment vs. control group as well as their interaction as independent variables.
These analyses show that participants' random assignment to a control or treatment group did not influence our results (see Tables S5-S6).
text.formatted: These analyses show that participants' random assignment to a control or treatment group did not influence our results (see Tables <ref type="table">S5-S6</ref>).

text.text: Measures.
We measured pluralistic ignorance as the averaged discrepancy between participants' own beliefs and their perceived beliefs of Swiss citizens.

Specifically, we used two discrete survey questions to assess participants' own views and their perceptions of others' views, which is recommended in the literature on pluralistic ignorance (Sargent & Newman, 2021) because discrete questioning produces the most comprehensible and comprehensive results and is recommended for studies with a within-subject design.
text.formatted: Specifically, we used two discrete survey questions to assess participants' own views and their perceptions of others' views, which is recommended in the literature on pluralistic ignorance <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Sargent & Newman, 2021)</ref> because discrete questioning produces the most comprehensible and comprehensive results and is recommended for studies with a within-subject design.

text.text: The same questions were asked pre-and post-referendum: Procedure.

After answering questions on their own and others' climate change concern and others' support for scientists' advocacy in the pre-referendum survey, participants were randomly assigned to a control or a treatment condition (note that assignment to a treatment or control condition was for a different study).
Participants then answered a question on their own support for scientists' policy advocacy.
In the post-referendum survey, participants were informed about the voting outcome in their canton of residence.
Participants in the treatment group additionally received a treatment reminder ("59.1 % of Swiss voters approved the Climate Protection Law.
In a previous survey, we showed you a statement issued by 230+ scientists.
In this statement, scientists publicly supported the Climate Protection Law.
These scientists were therefore representing the majority opinion of the Swiss electorate.")
The results of this experiment are reported in a different study (Cologna et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The results of this experiment are reported in a different study <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Cologna et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were then asked about their own and others' concern about climate change and advocacy support.
The complete full questionnaires, the datasets, and code can be accessed on the OSF.
Given the within-subjects design of our study, we ran paired t-tests to test our hypotheses and pre-registered exploratory analyses.
Moreover, non-preregistered multilevel regression models with random intercepts across participants replicate our findings (see Tables S3 and S4).
text.formatted: Moreover, non-preregistered multilevel regression models with random intercepts across participants replicate our findings (see Tables <ref type="table">S3</ref> and <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Following Eisner et al., (2021), we further tested whether the referendum affected the gap between perceived advocacy support and concern and actual advocacy support and concern.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Eisner et al., (2021)</ref>, we further tested whether the referendum affected the gap between perceived advocacy support and concern and actual advocacy support and concern.

text.text: This allowed us to inspect whether the referendum reduced this gap using paired t-tests on the level of discrepancy.
These analyses only include participants that participated in both the pre-and post-referendum survey.
We asked participants about their own level of concern about climate change as well as other people's concern in Switzerland.

As hypothesized, pre-referendum participants significantly underestimated others' concern about climate change (actual: N = 1,578, M = 3.78, SD = 1.08, perceived: N = 1,578, M = 3.39, SD = 0.76, difference: 95% CI of mean difference [0.33-0.44], t(1577) = 13.41, d = .34, p < .001).
text.formatted: As hypothesized, pre-referendum participants significantly underestimated others' concern about climate change (actual: N = 1,578, M = 3.78, SD = 1.08, perceived: N = 1,578, M = 3.39, SD = 0.76, difference: 95% CI of mean difference [0.33-0.44], t(1577) = 13.41, d = .34, p < .001).

text.text: Although this small discrepancy remained after the referendum (actual: N = 827, M = 3.76, SD = 1.13, perceived: N = 827, M = 3.55, SD = 0.78, 95% CI of mean difference [0.13 -0.29], t(826) = 5.42, d = .19, p < .001), comparing the responses of participants who completed both surveys before and after the referendum, we observe that others' perceived climate change concern significantly increased from before the referendum (N = 827, M = 3.38, SD = 0.78) to after the referendum (N = 827, M = 3.55, SD = 0.78 ; 95% CI of mean difference [0.11-0.22], t(826) = 5.85, d = .20, p < .001), leading to a significantly smaller discrepancy gap between perceived and actual concern post-referendum (t(826) = 4.17, d = .15, p < .001).
text.formatted: Although this small discrepancy remained after the referendum (actual: N = 827, M = 3.76, SD = 1.13, perceived: N = 827, M = 3.55, SD = 0.78, 95% CI of mean difference [0.13 -0.29], t(826) = 5.42, d = .19, p < .001), comparing the responses of participants who completed both surveys before and after the referendum, we observe that others' perceived climate change concern significantly increased from before the referendum (N = 827, M = 3.38, SD = 0.78) to after the referendum (N = 827, M = 3.55, SD = 0.78 ; 95% CI of mean difference [0.11-0.22], t(826) = 5.85, d = .20, p < .001), leading to a significantly smaller discrepancy gap between perceived and actual concern post-referendum (t(826) = 4.17, d = .15, p < .001).

text.text: In other words, participants' perceptions grew closer to the actual levels of concern, thus reducing pluralistic ignorance (Figure 1a-1b, see also Table S3).
text.formatted: In other words, participants' perceptions grew closer to the actual levels of concern, thus reducing pluralistic ignorance (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1a</ref>-1b, see also Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: However, these effect sizes are small and the dispersion of individual estimates remained similar.

Concerning support for scientists' policy advocacy ("Scientists should advocate for specific policies"), as hypothesized, we found a similar, small gap between participants' actual support and their perceptions of others' support pre-referendum (actual: N = 1,578, M = 3.53, SD = 1.11, perceived: N = 1,578, M = 3.38, SD = 0.98, difference: 95% CI of mean difference [0.10, 0.21], t(1577) = 5.40, d = .14, p < .001).
text.formatted: Concerning support for scientists' policy advocacy ("Scientists should advocate for specific policies"), as hypothesized, we found a similar, small gap between participants' actual support and their perceptions of others' support pre-referendum (actual: N = 1,578, M = 3.53, SD = 1.11, perceived: N = 1,578, M = 3.38, SD = 0.98, difference: 95% CI of mean difference [0.10, 0.21], t(1577) = 5.40, d = .14, p < .001).

text.text: This small difference persists after the referendum (actual: N = 827, M = 3.44, SD = 1.18, perceived: N = 827, M = 3.31, SD = 0.93, difference: 95% CI of mean difference [0.05, 0.20], t(826) = 3.22, d = .11, p = .001).
However, the effect sizes are negligible.

Among participants who completed both surveys before and after the referendum, we see that others' perceptions of advocacy thus remains unchanged among the same participants before (N = 827, M = 3.34, SD = 0.98) and after (N = 827, M = 3.31, SD = 0.93) the referendum (95% CI of mean difference [-0.09, 0.04], t(826) = -0.69, d = -.02, p = .491; Figure 2a-2b, see also Table S4), as did the discrepancy between perceived advocacy support and actual advocacy support pre and post referendum (t(826) = 1.012, d = .04, p = .312).
text.formatted: Among participants who completed both surveys before and after the referendum, we see that others' perceptions of advocacy thus remains unchanged among the same participants before (N = 827, M = 3.34, SD = 0.98) and after (N = 827, M = 3.31, SD = 0.93) the referendum (95% CI of mean difference [-0.09, 0.04], t(826) = -0.69, d = -.02, p = .491; Figure <ref type="figure">2a-2b</ref>, see also Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>), as did the discrepancy between perceived advocacy support and actual advocacy support pre and post referendum (t(826) = 1.012, d = .04, p = .312).

text.text: Our findings suggest that the high level of public support and acceptance of the referendum signaled other peoples' concern about climate change to participants, who then updated their beliefs about others.

However, the voting outcome tells people little about others' views on scientists' advocacy, which participants did not respond to in terms of updating their beliefs after observing the outcome of the referendum.  advocacy pre-and post-referendum.
Figure 2b: Discrepancy between perceived and actual support for scientists' policy advocacy pre and post referendum.
Overall, participants exhibited pluralistic ignorance regarding their fellow citizens' concerns about climate change and their support for scientists' advocacy.
However, misperceptions about others' concerns about climate change were slightly reduced after the acceptance of the climate change referendum.

Observing the outcome of the referendum (with a clear majority of "YES" votes) likely provided participants with concrete information about the views of others-or at least signals of others' views-and may have corrected misperceptions about the general public's attitudes toward climate change.

In contrast, participants' misperceptions about others' support for scientists' advocacy remained unchanged after the referendum, possibly hampering an important channel through which people's views on climate change may be influenced.

To show misperceptions of others' concern about climate change, we compared beliefs about others' concern to the concern individuals in our sample reported (and do the same for support for policy advocacy).

We recruited a large sample that is representative of the Swiss population in terms of age, gender, and tertiary education, but may not be exactly representative for income and political orientation (see Table S1).
text.formatted: We recruited a large sample that is representative of the Swiss population in terms of age, gender, and tertiary education, but may not be exactly representative for income and political orientation (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: Thus, survey respondents might not hold the same beliefs as the Swiss population-a clear limitation of our study that future research should tackle.
However, despite this limitation, we believe that it is a fair comparison to rate the accuracy of people's predictions with the data from our survey.

The fact that our study confirms findings from previous studies (i.e., pluralistic ignorance on climate change, see Andre et al., 2024; Dechezleprêtre et al., 2022; N. Geiger & Swim, 2016) additionally confirms the validity of the results.
text.formatted: The fact that our study confirms findings from previous studies (i.e., pluralistic ignorance on climate change, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Andre et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dechezleprêtre et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">N. Geiger & Swim, 2016)</ref> additionally confirms the validity of the results.

text.text: These observations have important implications for researchers and policymakers alike.

Since misperceptions about others' beliefs and values can influence peoples' own attitudes and behaviors, correcting misperceptions about others' climate change concerns may be an important channel for fostering more sustainable behaviors.

Thus, this robust evidence from a field setting around a national referendum in Switzerland underlines the value of climate policy votes for policy change as well as improving accuracy in peoples' perceptions of others' beliefs.
The Climate Protection Law may have been especially effective in decreasing pluralistic ignorance given the strong public support for the policy and widespread media attention.

Indeed, a study in Switzerland (Eisner et al., 2021) that analyzed pluralistic ignorance regarding the approval of same-sex parenting and marriage found that the introduction of a new law implemented by parliament (i.e., without popular voting) to promote the rights of same-sex couples-which did not get widespread media coverage-did not reduce pluralistic ignorance.
text.formatted: Indeed, a study in Switzerland <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Eisner et al., 2021)</ref> that analyzed pluralistic ignorance regarding the approval of same-sex parenting and marriage found that the introduction of a new law implemented by parliament (i.e., without popular voting) to promote the rights of same-sex couples-which did not get widespread media coverage-did not reduce pluralistic ignorance.

text.text: Future studies should analyze how media reporting and exposure affects pluralistic ignorance in the context of a national referendum.
We also recommend future research to address issues of social desirability bias related to the use of discrete measurements of pluralistic ignorance.

In conclusion, our study focused on one policy in one country, and replicating these results for other climate policies in other countries could meaningfully expand the scope of the current investigation.

Therefore, the Harvard University Area Committee on the Use of Human Subjects determined that no further ethics approval was needed for this study.
All subjects gave informed consent.
